# [Marler Blog](https://www.marlerblog.com)

Providing Insight on Food Poisoning Outbreaks & Litigation



# E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria Oh My!

By [Bill Marler](http://www.marlerclark.com/lawyers/view/william-marler) on

Posted in [Case News](https://www.marlerblog.com/articles/case-news/)

2024 has been a long and winding road of outbreak after outbreak and we still have a few more weeks.

**Iceberg and Romaine Lettuce *E. coli* Outbreak**

The FDA and CDC, in collaboration with state and local partners are investigating illnesses in a multistate outbreak of *E. coli* O157 (ref #1280) infections linked to an iceberg and romaine lettuce blend served at catering events, restaurants, and a school. Based on epidemiological information collected by CDC, a total of 69 people infected with the same strain of *E. coli* O157 have been reported from 10 states. FDA’s traceback investigation has identified an iceberg and romaine lettuce blend from a common supplier as the source of this outbreak; however, impacted product identified to date appears to be past shelf life and no longer on the market. FDA is continuing to work with the supplier to determine if any additional product could be impacted. At this time, there does not appear to be any ongoing risk to public health and there is no recommendation for consumers to avoid iceberg or romaine lettuce. FDA’s investigation is ongoing, and more information will be provided as it becomes available. This outbreak may well be linked to the Andre’s Catering *E. coli* Outbreak.

**Andre’s Catering *E. coli* Outbreak**

Missouri Health officials have reported that 115 people, including students from Rockwood Summit High School and adults from the community, have been confirmed as outbreak patients. The patients attended five separate events catered by Andre’s Banquet Center. Patients attended two school band events, two funerals and a Veterans’ event catered by the business. As of Nov. 21, county hospitals reported that two of the outbreak patients had developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS, a rare but serious disease that can occur as a complication of an *E. coli* infection.

**SunFed Cucumber *Salmonella* Outbreak**

As of November 26, 2024, a total of 68 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Salmonella* have been reported from 19 states: Alaska, California, Colorado, Iowa, Illinois, Massachusetts, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming.  Of the 50 people for whom information is available, 18 have been hospitalized. No deaths have been reported. On Thanksgiving Day, The whole fresh American cucumbers were sold by SunFed and other importers and shipped to customers located in the states of Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin & Wyoming and the Canadian provinces of Alberta, British Columbia, Calgary, Saskatchewan, & Ontario. On November 27, 2024, SunFed Produce, LLC initiated a recall of all sizes of American/slicer cucumbers that were grown by Agrotato, S.A. de C.V. in Sonora, Mexico.

**Yu Shang Food *Listeria*Outbreak**

As of November 22, 2024, 11 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Listeria*have been reported from four states: California (7), Illinois (2), New York (1) and New Jersey (1). Sick people’s samples were collected from October 24, 2021, to July 31, 2024. Of 11 people with information available, nine have been hospitalized. In California, one pregnant person and their twins were sick and both infants died. *Listeria*was found in a sample from the mother and from one of the twin infants, but it could not be found in a sample from the other infant. One other Listeria illness was reported in an infant who was sick and recovered. On November 9, 2024, Yu Shang Food, Inc recalled ready-to-eat meat and poultry products. On November 21, 2024, Yu Shang Food, Inc expanded their recall. CDC is advising people not to eat, sell, or serve recalled products.

**Grimmway Carrots *E. coli*Outbreak**

As of November 17, 2024, 39 people infected with the outbreak strain of *E. coli* have been reported from 18 states according to the CDC: Wyoming 1, Washington 8, Virginia 1, Texas 1, South Carolina 2, Pennsylvania 1, Oregon 3, Ohio 1, North Carolina 1, New York 5, New Jersey 2, Missouri 1, Minnesota 5, Michigan 1, Massachusetts 1, Colorado 1, California 3 and Arkansas 1. Illnesses started on dates ranging from September 6, 2024 to October 28, 2024. Of 38 people with information available, 15 have been hospitalized and none developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition that can cause kidney failure. One death has been reported from California. CDC and public health officials in several states are investigating a multistate outbreak of *E. coli* O121 infections linked to multiple brands of recalled organic whole bagged carrots and baby carrots sold by Grimmway Farms. Carrots on store shelves right now are likely not affected but may be in people’s homes.

**Wolverine Packing *E. coli* Outbreak**

At least 19 people in Minnesota have been sickened by *E. coli* O157 tied to a national recall of more than 167,000 pounds of potentially tainted ground beef. FSIS was notified of illnesses on November 13, 2024, and working in conjunction with Minnesota Departments of Agriculture and Health, FSIS determined that there was a link between the ground beef products from Wolverine Packing Co. and this illness cluster. On November 20, 2024, a ground beef sample collected by the Minnesota Department of Agriculture as part of an outbreak investigation tested positive for *E. coli*O157. To date, case-patients have been identified in Minnesota with illness onset dates ranging from November 2, 2024, to November 10, 2024. The infections occurred in people who had eaten hamburgers at Red Cow restaurants in the Minneapolis and Rochester areas, as well as the Hen House Eatery in Minneapolis.

**McDonald’s *E. coli* Outbreak**

As of November 13, 2024, 104 people infected with the outbreak strain of *E. coli*O157:H7 have been reported from 14 states: Colorado 30, Montana 19, Wyoming 6, Kansas 3, North Carolina 1, Iowa 1, Missouri 8, Michigan 1, Nebraska 12, New Mexico 10, Oregon 1, Utah 8, Washington 1 and Wisconsin 1. Of 98 people with information available, 34 have been hospitalized, and 4 people developed HUS, a serious condition that can cause kidney failure. One death has been reported from an older adult in Colorado. This person is not one of those who developed HUS. Of the 81 people interviewed, 80 (99%) report eating at McDonald’s. Seventy-five people were able to remember specific menu items they ate at McDonald’s. 63 of 75 people (84%) reported a menu item containing Taylor Farm’s fresh slivered onions.

**Milo’s Poultry Farms Egg *Salmonella* Outbreak**

As of October 17, 2024, a total of 93 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Salmonella*have been reported from 12 states: Arizona, California, Iowa, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Utah, Virginia and Colorado. Illnesses started on dates ranging from May 23, 2024, to September 13, 2024. Of 87 people with information available, 34 have been hospitalized and no deaths have been reported. The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade, and Consumer Protection traced the source of eggs supplied to restaurants where ill people ate before they got sick. Records show that Milo’s Poultry Farms supplied eggs to those restaurants. FDA conducted an inspection at Milo’s Poultry Farms and collected samples. The outbreak strain of *Salmonella* was found in the packing facility, the hen egg laying house, and in recalled eggs.

**Boar’s Head*Listeria* Outbreak**

As of November 19, a total of 61 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Listeria*were reported from 19 states: Arizona 1, Florida 3, Georgia 2, Illinois 1, Indiana 1, Louisiana 1, Massachusetts 3, Maryland 8, Minnesota 1, Missouri 3, North Carolina 1, New Jersey 6, New Mexico 1, New York 19, Pennsylvania 2, South Carolina 2, Tennessee 1, Virginia 4 and Wisconsin 1. Sick people’s samples were collected from May 29, 2024, to September 13, 2024. Of 61 people with information available, 60 were hospitalized. One person got sick during their pregnancy and remained pregnant after recovering. Ten deaths were reported, including one in Illinois, one in New Jersey, two in New York, one in Virginia, one in Florida, one in Tennessee, one in New Mexico, and two in South Carolina. Epidemiologic, laboratory, and traceback data showed that meats sliced at deli counters, including Boar’s Head brand liverwurst, were contaminated with *Listeria* and made people sick.

**Wagyu Beef *E. coli* Outbreak**

The Flathead City-County Health Department (FCCHD) and the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) worked to investigate an *E. coli*O157:H7 outbreak originating in Flathead County. Illnesses have been reported in Montana residents as well as people who visited Montana over the 4th of July week including Arizona, Oregon, Wyoming, Florida, Virginia and Canada.  On July 25th, FCCHD and DPHHS received confirmatory testing results of clinical and food samples verifying ground beef as the exposure of concern. Specifically, the source of the outbreak was wagyu beef from one lot number. All cases reported eating undercooked or made-to-order burgers made with wagyu beef at one of multiple restaurants in Flathead County. The last known date of consumption was July 14, 2024. The following restaurants are associated with the 22 cases of reported illness in this outbreak: Gunsight Saloon; Hops Downtown Grill; Tamarack Brewing Company; the Lodge at Whitefish Lake; and Harbor Grille. Two individuals have died after exposure to wagyu beef consumed at various restaurants.

**Raw Milk *Salmonella* Outbreak**

On October 18, 2023, an investigation of an outbreak associated with Raw Farm, LLC products was initiated. At least eight *Salmonella* cases who had reported consuming raw milk from Raw Farm, LLC of Fresno County, California, were discovered and reported to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH). As of October 15, 2024, 171 cases (159 confirmed and 12 probable) have been reported from five states: CA (167), NM (1), TX (1), WA (1), and PA (1). In California the following counties reported cases: Los Angeles (27), San Diego (25), Orange (19), Placer (7),Riverside (7), Sacramento (7), Alameda (6), Ventura (6), Contra Costa (5), Kern (5), San Bernardino (5), Santa Clara (5), Solano (5), Santa Barbara (4), Stanislaus (4), Long Beach (4), Fresno (3), Kings (2), Madera (2), Nevada (2), San Joaquin (2), and Yolo (2). Illness onsets ranged from September 21 to March 12, 2024. Symptoms included fever, bloody or watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and headache. The age range of cases was <1 to 87 years (median 7). Sixty-five percent of cases were male. Twenty cases (14%) were known to require hospitalization; no deaths were reported. Four cases were discovered to have co-infections with *S.*Typhimurium and *Campylobacter*and/or STEC. Most illnesses were among children.

# Investigation Update: Salmonella Outbreak, Eggs - September 2024

## Key points

This outbreak is over. Recalled eggs are no longer available for sale and are outside their shelf life.

![Carton of eggs](/salmonella/eggs-09-24/images/GettyImages-1356240873.jpg "Closeup macro of pasture raised farm fresh dozen brown eggs store bought from farmer in carton box container with speckled eggshells texture")

## October 17, 2024

CDC, public health and regulatory officials in several states, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) collected [different types of data](https://www.cdc.gov/foodborne-outbreaks/about-data/index.html) to investigate a multistate outbreak of *Salmonella* Enteritidis infections**.**

Epidemiologic, laboratory, and traceback data showed that eggs supplied by Milo's Poultry Farms were contaminated with *Salmonella* and made people sick.

### Epidemiologic data

As of October 17, 2024, a total of 93 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Salmonella* have been reported from 12 states. Illnesses started on dates ranging from May 23, 2024, to September 13, 2024. Of 87 people with information available, 34 have been hospitalized and no deaths have been reported.

The true number of sick people in this outbreak was likely much higher than the number reported, and the outbreak may not have been limited to the states with known illnesses. This is because many people recover without medical care and are not tested for *Salmonella*.

Public health officials collected many different types of information from sick people, including their age, race, ethnicity, other demographics, and the foods they ate in the week before they got sick. This information provided clues to help investigators identify the source of the outbreak.

The table below has information about sick people in this outbreak ("n" is the number of people with information available for each demographic).

**Demographics**

State and local public health officials interviewed people about the foods they ate in the week before they got sick. Several sick people reported eating at the same restaurants before getting sick. These illness clusters provided clues about what food item made people sick. If several unrelated sick people ate or shopped at the same location of a restaurant or store within several days of each other, it suggests that the contaminated food item was served or sold there. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services identified three illness clusters at restaurants where eggs were served.

### Laboratory and traceback data

Public health investigators used the [PulseNet](https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html) system to identify illnesses that may be part of this outbreak. CDC PulseNet manages a national database of DNA fingerprints of bacteria that cause foodborne illnesses. DNA fingerprinting is performed on bacteria using a method called [whole genome sequencing (WGS)](/pulsenet/php/wgs/index.html). WGS showed that bacteria from sick peoples' samples are closely related genetically. This suggests that people in this outbreak got sick from the same food.

The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade, and Consumer Protection traced the source of eggs supplied to restaurants where ill people ate before they got sick. Records show that Milo's Poultry Farms supplied eggs to those restaurants.

FDA conducted an inspection at Milo's Poultry Farms and collected samples. The outbreak strain of *Salmonella* was found in the packing facility, the hen egg laying house, and in recalled eggs.

Based on [WGS analysis](https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/php/wgs/index.html), bacteria from 83 people's samples and 72 environmental samples are predicted to be nonsusceptible to ciprofloxacin and are related to a strain of *Salmonella* Enteritidis that has also been isolated from chicken. Most people with *Salmonella* illness recover without antibiotics. However, if antibiotics are needed, illnesses in this outbreak may be difficult to treat with some commonly recommended antibiotics and may require a different antibiotic choice. More information is available at the [National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS)](https://www.cdc.gov/narms/index.html) site.

### Public health actions

Milo's Poultry Farm recalled all eggs supplied by their farm. Recalled eggs are past shelf life and should no longer be available for sale.

The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade, and Consumer Protection traced the source of eggs supplied to restaurants where ill people ate before they got sick. Records show that Milo's Poultry Farms supplied eggs to those restaurants.

FDA conducted an inspection at Milo's Poultry Farms and collected samples. FDA's analysis showed the outbreak strain of *Salmonella* was found in the packing facility and the hen egg laying house.

[WGS analysis](https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/php/wgs/index.html) of bacteria from 65 people's samples showed predicted resistance to nalidixic acid and ciprofloxacin. More information is available at the [National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS)](https://www.cdc.gov/narms/index.html) site. Most people with *Salmonella* illness recover without antibiotics. However, if antibiotics are needed, illnesses in this outbreak may be difficult to treat with some commonly recommended antibiotics and may require a different antibiotic choice.

#### Public Health Actions

On September 6, 2024, Milo's Poultry Farms recalled eggs. CDC is advising people not eat, sell, or serve recalled eggs.

# Investigation Update: Salmonella Outbreak, Cucumbers, November 2024

## Key points

This outbreak is over. Learn what you can do to protect yourself from getting sick from *Salmonella*.

![whole fresh American cucumbers](/salmonella/media/images/2024/11/SunFed-Cucumber.jpg "whole fresh American cucumbers")

## Latest update

### January 8, 2025

CDC, public health and regulatory officials in several states, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), collected [different types of data](https://www.cdc.gov/foodborne-outbreaks/about-data/index.html) to investigate a multistate outbreak of *Salmonella* Typhimurium infections**.**

Epidemiologic and traceback data showed that cucumbers grown by Agrotato, S.A. de C.V. in Sonora, Mexico, were contaminated with *Salmonella* and made people sick.

### Epidemiologic Data

A total of 113 people infected with the outbreak strain of *Salmonella* were reported from 23 states. Illnesses started on dates ranging from October 12, 2024, to December 7, 2024. Of the 99 people for whom information was available, 28 were hospitalized. No deaths were reported.

The true number of sick people in this outbreak was likely much higher than the number reported, and the outbreak may not have been limited to the states with known illnesses. This is because many people recover without medical care and are not tested for *Salmonella*.

Public health officials collected many different types of information from sick people, including their age, race, ethnicity, other demographics, and the foods they ate in the week before they got sick. This information provided clues to help investigators identify the source of the outbreak.

The table below has information about sick people in this outbreak ("n" is the number of people with information available for each demographic).

State and local public health officials interviewed people about the foods they ate in the week before they got sick. Of the 69 people interviewed, 56 (81%) reported eating or likely eating cucumbers. This percentage was significantly higher than the 50% of respondents who reported eating cucumbers in the [FoodNet Population Survey](https://www.cdc.gov/foodnet/surveys/population.html)**—**a survey that helps estimate how often people eat various foods linked to diarrheal illness. This difference suggests that people in this outbreak got sick from eating cucumbers.

CDC and states identified seven illness sub-clusters at three assisted living facilities, three school districts, and one restaurant. An illness sub-cluster is a group of unrelated sick people who all ate at the same location or event, such as a restaurant, long-term care facility, or school. Investigating sub-clusters can help identify a food item eaten by all the sick people that could be the source of the outbreak. Cucumbers were served at all seven sub-cluster locations.

### Laboratory and Traceback Data

Public health investigators used the [PulseNet](https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html) system to identify illnesses that may have been part of this outbreak. CDC PulseNet manages a national database of DNA fingerprints of bacteria that cause foodborne illnesses. DNA fingerprinting is performed on bacteria using a method called [whole genome sequencing (WGS)](/pulsenet/php/wgs/index.html). WGS showed that bacteria from sick people's samples were closely related genetically. This suggests that people in this outbreak got sick from the same food.

[WGS analysis](https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/php/wgs/index.html) of 109 people's samples did not predict resistance to any antibiotics. More information is available at the [National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS)](https://www.cdc.gov/narms/index.html) site.

People reported eating cucumbers at different restaurants and sub-cluster locations or buying cucumbers from multiple stores. FDA's traceback investigation identified Agrotato, S.A. de C.V. in Sonora, Mexico as a common grower of cucumbers.

### Public Health Actions

Many companies recalled cucumbers or foods made with them. The products are no longer available for sale.

# *Salmonella* Outbreak Linked to Cucumbers - June 2024

## Food safety alert

This outbreak is over. Learn what you can do to protect yourself from getting sick from *Salmonella*.

## Fast Facts

## Outbreak investigation summary

This outbreak is over. Epidemiologic, traceback, and laboratory data showed that cucumbers were contaminated with *Salmonella* and made people sick. Testing identified the *Salmonella* Braenderup outbreak strain in untreated canal water used by a grower in Florida. An additional grower was identified as a likely source of illnesses in this outbreak. Cucumbers from both of these growers are no longer in season and products are no longer on shelves.

### Recalled Food

Fresh Start Produce Sales Inc. issued a [recall](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts/fresh-start-produce-sales-initiates-recall-whole-cucumbers-because-possible-health-risk) of whole cucumbers due to the potential of being contaminated with *Salmonella*. Recalled cucumbers did not account for all the illnesses in this outbreak.

## What you should do

**Follow these [four food safety steps](https://www.foodsafety.gov/keep-food-safe/4-steps-to-food-safety#chill) to prevent getting sick from *Salmonella*.**

# Salmonella By the Numbers

[The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that *Salmonella* is responsible for 1.35 million infections, 26,500 hospitalizations, and 420 deaths in the United States every year](https://www.cdc.gov/salmonella/index.html#:~:text=CDC%20estimates%20Salmonella%20bacteria%20cause,%2C%20fever%2C%20and%20stomach%20cramps.). Food is the source of most of these illnesses, and the [Interagency Food Safety Analytics Collaboration estimates that over 23% of foodborne *Salmonella* illnesses are due to eating chicken and turkey](https://www.cdc.gov/foodsafety/ifsac/pdf/P19-2019-report-TriAgency-508.pdf).

FSIS testing data show that *Salmonella* contamination on poultry has been going down, but this has not translated into a reduction in human illnesses. Rates of human illness have remained stagnant over the last two decades, and we have not moved any closer to the [national goal of a 25% reduction in *Salmonella* illnesses](https://health.gov/healthypeople/objectives-and-data/browse-objectives/foodborne-illness).

All of this data points toward the need for a new approach to controlling *Salmonella* in poultry in a way that reduces human *Salmonella* illnesses. These are just a few of the references and research articles we are considering as we look to develop a revised framework for *Salmonella* control in poultry.

selection_manifest.human_review_reason:
This source is a live search result pointing to an FDA.gov outbreak investigation page for Salmonella linked to cucumbers, dated November 2024. The domain authority is very high (fda.gov, 0.95) and disease relevance is strong (0.95, confirmed Salmonella match). However, several factors constrain its utility for this specific collection task:

1. **Temporal mismatch**: The page title explicitly states "November 2024," while the collection window is 2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31. This is the primary driver of reduced relevance — the outbreak investigation page may describe an event outside the target window entirely, or may contain retrospective case data that partially overlaps. This is the most significant advisory concern.

2. **Role assignment tension**: The deterministic system assigned `context` role, but the domain is a primary authoritative public health source (FDA). The contradiction between `official_public_health_authority` and `secondary_news_or_media_source` flags — both present simultaneously — indicates a classification conflict that warrants LLM review. The `screening_and_critic_disagree` flag confirms this.

3. **Missing publisher field**: While the domain is unambiguously FDA, the null publisher field is a minor provenance gap that should be resolved during extraction.

4. **Geographic granularity**: Score of 0.58 suggests the page likely reports national-level aggregate data without subnational breakdown, limiting its utility for locality-level required fields.

5. **Source type mismatch**: Classified as `news_and_situation_report` despite originating from fda.gov. FDA outbreak investigation pages are typically official public health agency outputs and should likely be reclassified as `official_public_health_agency` — this reclassification would elevate its priority tier in the collection spec.

6. **Data signal present but unverified**: Three data signals were detected in metadata, but no snippet is available. The actual page content has not been retrieved, so case counts, dates, and locations cannot be confirmed from metadata alone.

However, several critical issues substantially reduce its utility for this specific collection task:

1. **Disease relevance is critically low (0.10):** The deterministic assessment found zero target-disease terms (e.g., "Salmonella") in the available source text. The title references "foodborne illness outbreaks" generically, not Salmonella specifically. This is the dominant driver of the low composite credibility score (0.52).

2. **Source type mismatch:** The source is tagged as `news_and_situation_report`, but it is hosted on PMC, strongly suggesting it is a peer-reviewed or policy/review article. This is the lowest-priority source type in the collection spec's `source_priority` hierarchy, and the type label itself may be incorrect — a peer-reviewed article would rank higher but still below official public health agency outputs.

3. **Content focus is regulatory/policy, not epidemiological:** The title signals a policy analysis or review article about regulatory responses, not a primary epidemiological report containing case counts, outbreak dates, hospitalizations, or deaths. It is unlikely to directly populate required fields such as `cases_confirmed`, `deaths`, `hospitalizations`, or `date_reported`.

4. **Temporal alignment is uncertain:** The timeliness_score (0.72) is moderate. PMC article PMC12855058 has a high article ID number suggesting recent publication, but the article's internal data coverage period is unknown from metadata alone. It may reference historical outbreaks rather than the 2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31 target window.

5. **Contradictory risk flags:** The flag set contains mutually contradictory signals — e.g., `official_public_health_authority` vs. `secondary_news_or_media_source`, and `primary_or_authoritative_source` vs. `ambiguous_disease` and `screening_and_critic_disagree`. This internal inconsistency warrants caution and suggests the deterministic pipeline had difficulty classifying this source cleanly.

6. **No snippet available:** With `snippet: null`, there is no extractable text to confirm disease relevance, data signals, or time window coverage. Any collection attempt would require full-text retrieval and manual review.

**Summary:** The platform is credible, but the source itself is almost certainly a policy/regulatory review article with no direct Salmonella case data for the target window. It should be held as `context` only and not used for primary data extraction without human confirmation of content.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify CDC outbreak investigation pages, CDC FoodNet surveillance reports, and CDC PulseNet cluster announcements reporting Salmonella human cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in the United States during May–July 2024.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: CDC is the primary US federal public health authority for Salmonella surveillance. FoodNet provides active case counts; PulseNet tracks WGS-linked clusters; outbreak investigation pages provide serotype-specific case, hospitalization, and death counts with dates and locations.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify FDA CFSAN outbreak and food safety alert pages that report human illness counts, hospitalizations, and deaths linked to Salmonella-contaminated food products recalled or investigated during May–July 2024.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: FDA CFSAN publishes outbreak investigation pages with case counts, states affected, and illness date ranges for foodborne Salmonella events, often complementing CDC data.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify state health department situation reports, press releases, and epidemiological bulletins from US states reporting Salmonella case counts, hospitalizations, or deaths during May–July 2024.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: State health departments (e.g., California CDPH, Texas DSHS, Florida DOH) publish subnational Salmonella data that may not be aggregated at the federal level within the task time window.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify USDA FSIS outbreak investigation reports that include human illness case counts linked to meat, poultry, or egg products during May–July 2024.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: USDA FSIS investigates Salmonella outbreaks linked to FSIS-regulated products and publishes human illness counts alongside recall notices.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify WHO PAHO situation reports or event-based surveillance summaries covering Salmonella outbreaks in the United States during 2024 for independent cross-validation of case and death counts.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: PAHO and WHO publish regional disease event summaries that can serve as independent validation against CDC-reported figures.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify CDC NORS (National Outbreak Reporting System) data or summary tables for Salmonella outbreaks reported in 2024 to cross-validate outbreak-level case and death counts.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: NORS is a structured database of US foodborne and enteric disease outbreaks; its aggregate counts can validate individual outbreak records collected from other sources.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify CDC case definition documents and FoodNet methodology pages to clarify count semantics (confirmed vs. probable vs. suspected) and reporting lag for Salmonella surveillance in the US.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Understanding CDC case definitions and FoodNet active surveillance methodology is essential for correctly classifying extracted counts into the appropriate schema fields.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify peer-reviewed literature (PubMed/MMWR) reporting Salmonella outbreak investigations or surveillance summaries for the United States in 2024 to provide epidemiological context and case definition clarity.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: MMWR reports and peer-reviewed outbreak investigations provide detailed case definitions, serotype data, and epidemiological curves that contextualize extracted counts.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify reputable news and situation report sources (e.g., Outbreak News Today, Food Safety News, ProMED) covering Salmonella outbreaks in the United States during May–July 2024 to surface outbreak signals not yet reflected in official sources.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: News and situation reports may capture early outbreak signals, state-level case counts, or recall-linked illness data before official CDC pages are published.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Flag sources where count semantics are ambiguous (e.g., cumulative vs. newly reported), where the reporting period substantially exceeds May–July 2024, or where Salmonella counts may include typhoidal serotypes, for human review before extraction.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Ambiguous count semantics, broad reporting periods, and typhoidal contamination are the primary risks for incorrect record extraction in this task.

planned_source_categories.why_relevant: CDC Division of Foodborne, Waterborne, and Environmental Diseases (DFWED) publishes multistate Salmonella outbreak investigation pages with serotype, case counts, hospitalization counts, death counts, illness date ranges, and states affected. These are the highest-priority collection sources for the task.

CDC FoodNet (Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network) provides active laboratory-confirmed Salmonella case counts across 10 US sites. Annual and preliminary reports may contain 2024 data covering the task window.
CDC PulseNet tracks WGS-linked Salmonella clusters and publishes cluster announcements with case counts and states affected. Relevant for identifying outbreak-linked confirmed case counts.
FDA CFSAN outbreak investigation pages report human illness counts, hospitalizations, and deaths linked to Salmonella-contaminated FDA-regulated food products. Often published alongside food recalls.

US state health departments publish Salmonella outbreak reports, press releases, and epidemiological bulletins with subnational case counts, hospitalizations, and deaths. Key states include CA, TX, FL, NY, GA, WA, and others with high Salmonella burden.
USDA FSIS publishes outbreak investigation reports and recall notices for Salmonella linked to meat, poultry, and egg products, including human illness counts.
PAHO and WHO publish regional disease event summaries and situation reports that may include US Salmonella outbreak data for independent cross-validation.
CDC NORS (National Outbreak Reporting System) is a structured database of US foodborne and enteric disease outbreaks with case, hospitalization, and death counts by pathogen, year, and state.

CDC MMWR reports and peer-reviewed outbreak investigations provide detailed Salmonella case definitions, serotype data, epidemiological curves, and case/death counts for US outbreaks. MMWR is the primary rapid communication vehicle for US outbreak investigations.

Reputable food safety and outbreak news sources (Food Safety News, Outbreak News Today, ProMED) may surface early Salmonella outbreak signals, state-level case counts, and recall-linked illness data before official CDC pages are finalized.

Confirmed in-window outbreaks with case counts, hospitalizations, and deaths: (a) Backyard Poultry May 2024 — 470 confirmed cases, 1 death, 48 states, illness onset Jan 1–Sep 4 2024 (CDC + CIDRAP); (b) Cucumbers June 2024 — CDC index page found, Salmonella Braenderup, Florida grower, recall issued (case counts not visible in snippet but page is surfaced for data collection); (c) Eggs Sep 2024 with illness onset May 23–Sep 13 2024 — 93 cases, 34 hospitalizations, 0 deaths, 12 states (CDC + CIDRAP). Gaps: cases_probable and cases_suspected fields remain largely uncovered (only 1 probable case noted in Bearded Dragons MMWR, which is outside the window); locality (sub-state) granularity absent; FDA/FSIS advisory pages with explicit case counts not surfaced; Fresh Basil April 2024 outbreak may have illness dates extending into May 2024 but no case counts visible in snippet.
iterative_source_discovery_summary.final_trustworthiness_assessment: High trustworthiness for the primary candidates. CDC outbreak investigation pages (cdc.gov) are the gold-standard authoritative source for confirmed US Salmonella case counts, hospitalizations, and deaths. CIDRAP articles directly cite CDC figures and add corroborating detail (e.g., 1 death in Illinois for backyard poultry, illness onset dates through July 26 for egg-linked outbreak). FoodNet preliminary data is an official CDC surveillance product. The 50% duplicate rate in iteration 2 reflects search engine saturation of the CDC domain for this query space, not a quality concern. No low-trust or non-authoritative sources are being recommended as primary evidence.

selection_manifest.human_review_reason:
This source is a live search result pointing to an FDA.gov outbreak investigation page for Salmonella linked to cucumbers, dated November 2024. The domain authority is very high (fda.gov, 0.95) and disease relevance is strong (0.95, confirmed Salmonella match). However, several factors constrain its utility for this specific collection task:

1. **Temporal mismatch**: The page title explicitly states "November 2024," while the collection window is 2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31. This is the primary driver of reduced relevance — the outbreak investigation page may describe an event outside the target window entirely, or may contain retrospective case data that partially overlaps. This is the most significant advisory concern.

2. **Role assignment tension**: The deterministic system assigned `context` role, but the domain is a primary authoritative public health source (FDA). The contradiction between `official_public_health_authority` and `secondary_news_or_media_source` flags — both present simultaneously — indicates a classification conflict that warrants LLM review. The `screening_and_critic_disagree` flag confirms this.

3. **Missing publisher field**: While the domain is unambiguously FDA, the null publisher field is a minor provenance gap that should be resolved during extraction.

4. **Geographic granularity**: Score of 0.58 suggests the page likely reports national-level aggregate data without subnational breakdown, limiting its utility for locality-level required fields.

5. **Source type mismatch**: Classified as `news_and_situation_report` despite originating from fda.gov. FDA outbreak investigation pages are typically official public health agency outputs and should likely be reclassified as `official_public_health_agency` — this reclassification would elevate its priority tier in the collection spec.

6. **Data signal present but unverified**: Three data signals were detected in metadata, but no snippet is available. The actual page content has not been retrieved, so case counts, dates, and locations cannot be confirmed from metadata alone.

**Advisory role suggestion**: Upgrade from `context` to `primary` if page content confirms case data falling within the 2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31 window upon retrieval. Retain as `context` if the outbreak is confirmed to be entirely post-July 2024. Human review is recommended to resolve the temporal overlap ambiguity and the source_type misclassification before extraction proceeds.

selection_manifest.human_review_reason:
This source is hosted on PubMed Central (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), a highly authoritative and reputable platform (authority_score=0.95), and its title — "Regulatory responses to foodborne illness outbreaks in the United States and their implications for food safety" — is geographically and topically adjacent to the collection task. However, several critical issues substantially reduce its utility for this specific collection task:

1. **Disease relevance is critically low (0.10):** The deterministic assessment found zero target-disease terms (e.g., "Salmonella") in the available source text. The title references "foodborne illness outbreaks" generically, not Salmonella specifically. This is the dominant driver of the low composite credibility score (0.52).

2. **Source type mismatch:** The source is tagged as `news_and_situation_report`, but it is hosted on PMC, strongly suggesting it is a peer-reviewed or policy/review article. This is the lowest-priority source type in the collection spec's `source_priority` hierarchy, and the type label itself may be incorrect — a peer-reviewed article would rank higher but still below official public health agency outputs.

3. **Content focus is regulatory/policy, not epidemiological:** The title signals a policy analysis or review article about regulatory responses, not a primary epidemiological report containing case counts, outbreak dates, hospitalizations, or deaths. It is unlikely to directly populate required fields such as `cases_confirmed`, `deaths`, `hospitalizations`, or `date_reported`.

4. **Temporal alignment is uncertain:** The timeliness_score (0.72) is moderate. PMC article PMC12855058 has a high article ID number suggesting recent publication, but the article's internal data coverage period is unknown from metadata alone. It may reference historical outbreaks rather than the 2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31 target window.

5. **Contradictory risk flags:** The flag set contains mutually contradictory signals — e.g., `official_public_health_authority` vs. `secondary_news_or_media_source`, and `primary_or_authoritative_source` vs. `ambiguous_disease` and `screening_and_critic_disagree`. This internal inconsistency warrants caution and suggests the deterministic pipeline had difficulty classifying this source cleanly.

6. **No snippet available:** With `snippet: null`, there is no extractable text to confirm disease relevance, data signals, or time window coverage. Any collection attempt would require full-text retrieval and manual review.

**Summary:** The platform is credible, but the source itself is almost certainly a policy/regulatory review article with no direct Salmonella case data for the target window. It should be held as `context` only and not used for primary data extraction without human confirmation of content.

FSNS (fsns.com) appears to be a food safety and nutrition services commercial entity, not an official public health agency or peer-reviewed outlet. The page title ("Food Recalls in 2024: Revealing the Statistics") is statistical/aggregative in nature and does not directly name Salmonella as the subject disease, yielding a very low disease relevance score (0.20) with zero target disease terms found in metadata. The authority score is modest (0.48), reflecting a non-governmental, commercially oriented domain. The independence score is low (0.42) and the publisher field is null, both of which reduce confidence in editorial independence and provenance transparency. The risk penalty (0.22) is meaningful. While the page may contain recall statistics that are tangentially relevant to Salmonella food safety context, it is not a primary epidemiological data source and should not be used for case, death, or hospitalization counts. The deterministic screener and critic disagree (flag: screening_and_critic_disagree), which warrants advisory caution. The source is appropriate only as background context, if at all, and any figures cited must be cross-validated against FDA, USDA FSIS, or CDC primary sources before use.

PIRG (Public Interest Research Group) is an advocacy and consumer watchdog organization, not a public health surveillance agency. The domain pirg.org carries moderate name recognition but low epidemiological authority for Salmonella case/outbreak data. The title "Food for Thought 2025" is a policy/advocacy report framing, not a surveillance or situation report. The document title year (2025) is misaligned with the collection time window (2024-05-01 to 2024-07-31), raising a temporal provenance concern. No target disease terms (Salmonella, salmonellosis, non-typhoidal Salmonella) were found in source metadata, and the disease relevance score is very low (0.20). The source was discovered via a live search result rather than a curated source list, and the publisher field is null, reducing provenance confidence. The independence score (0.42) is below threshold, consistent with an advocacy-origin document that may present selectively framed food safety statistics. The deterministic screener and critic disagree on role assignment (flag: screening_and_critic_disagree), which warrants advisory caution. The role hint and deterministic assignment of "context" is appropriate: this source should not be used as a primary case count or outbreak data source. If accessed, it may provide background on food safety policy or aggregate recall statistics, but any numerical claims would require cross-validation against CDC DFWED, FDA, or USDA FSIS primary sources. The missing publisher field and advocacy framing together elevate the risk of selectively reported or non-primary data being mistaken for surveillance figures.

Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. ![CDC Logo](/TemplatePackage/4.0/assets/imgs/logo/logo-notext.svg) ![CDC Logo](/TemplatePackage/4.0/assets/imgs/logo/logo-notext.svg) # Reoccurring *Salmonella* Cotham Outbreak Linked to Pet Bearded Dragons — United States, 2024 *Weekly* / August 21, 2025 / 74(31);474–479 Lingzi Xiaoli, PhD1; Paula Huth, MPH2; Cassandra Sherman, MPH3; Danielle Wroblewski, MS2; Stacy Anderson4; Lindsey Ferraro, MPH5; Dee Jones, DVM5; Molly Slaughter, MPH6; Brenda Morningstar, MS7; Tonya Mackie7; Natalee Bowen8; Molly Leeper, MPH1; Katie Werner, MPH1; Katharine Benedict, DVM, PhD1; Kate Varela, DVM1 ([View author affiliations](#contribAff)) ### **Summary** **What is already known about this topic?** Bearded dragons have been linked to *Salmonella* outbreaks, including a 2012–2014 *Salmonella* Cotham outbreak involving 160 patients in 35 states. **What is added by this report?** Twenty-seven cases (26 confirmed and one probable) of *S*. Cotham infection were identified during January 11–December 10, 2024. Eighteen reported cases were among persons with household exposure to bearded dragons; *S.* Cotham isolates from two bearded dragons kept in two patient households were closely genetically related to each other, to 2012–2014 isolates, and to clinical isolates from the 26 confirmed cases.
